Tiny House Aigoual Creates a Light-Filled Oasis in Less Than 250 Square Feet
16 photos
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois
The idea of an oasis-like private sanctuary filled with natural light typically brings to mind the kind of spacious, luxurious XL tiny homes that are so popular in the US, but it doesn’t necessarily have to be so. French artisans are experts at making even the most compact wooden mobile homes look and feel extra luminous, even with simple techniques.
Tiny house Aigoual looks a bit different than its sister tiny homes from the same builder, the Occitania-based Mon Reve en Bois. It proudly shows off the same traditional French house silhouette with a double-pitched roof, elegant windows, and natural timber cladding, yet the eye immediately goes to the silvery aluminum trims and rooftop – an unusual, unexpected style element that adds an urban edgy without clashing with the rustic aesthetic.
It makes tiny house Aigoual pop – you’ll notice it among a crowd of wooden tiny homes, and you’ll surely remember it afterwards. The discrete color of the aluminum trims, and the muted shine, complement the natural tone and texture of the Douglas pine exterior beautifully, staying in line with this builder’s minimalist, artisan aesthetic that bans anything artificial or flashy.
This isn’t just any regular timber, either. The Douglas pine and spruce are sourced exclusively from local, sustainably-managed woods in Occitania. This local wood is specifically chosen for its highly resinous composition that makes it naturally resistant to insects, the elements, and weather damage overall. It’s also easy to maintain long-term, not to mention the beautiful natural texture and tone that make almost every French tiny house so special.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois Relying on local, sustainably-sourced timber is one of the sustainable practices that this French builder strives to incorporate in the workshop’s everyday activity. They also recycle all the wood waste resulting from the building process, and try to opt for as many eco-friendly components as possible. Aside from the construction process itself, they encourage customers to opt for the autonomous kits that turn these rustic mobile homes into self-sufficient abodes.
A regular autonomy kit from this builder includes a solar energy system adapted to the size of the house, a waterless toilet, and a water storage tank plus the filtration system, but options go as far as a solar-powered water heater and a separate, exterior waterless toilet. A wider range of options means that tiny home owners with different needs and budgets can find the best way to fit these off-grid solutions into their new lifestyle – better for them and for the environment.
Size-wise, this particular model stays within the typical dimensions of wooden homes on wheels built in France, but the one-loft layout allows for generous accommodation. A standard 2.5-meter (8 feet) width coupled with less than 7 meters (23 feet) in length would lead you to believe that there’s not too much flexibility inside this home on wheels, yet you’d be surprised to find out not only that it can accommodate four people, but that it’s extra bright and airy as well.
From the outside, you can spot the big, romantic porthole-windows that bring more light to this tiny house as well as adding a touch of whimsy. You’ve surely seen tiny homes with one porthole added to the lounge or the loft bedroom as a style statement, but models with three rounded windows (aside from the regular ones) are quite unusual.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois Tiny house Aigoual has one in the lounge, right above the sofa, one in the loft bedroom above, and a third one in the kitchen, close to the main entrance. The visual effect is lovely, and nobody will complain about even more natural light finding its way to this timber interior. Strategically-placed windows along with a four-meter (13 feet) height are a classic solution for enhanced luminosity and airiness in a tiny house, and the portholes are the cherry on top.
In this space-efficient layout, the solid, custom-crafted staircase that leads to the main bedroom becomes the central part of the house, with the compact kitchen and bathroom on one side, and the open lounge on the other side. This placement creates separation between the two areas without blocking the flow – in other words, there’s balance between unobstructed movement around the house and the need for privacy.
Small, basic kitchens are the norm when it comes to French tiny homes. You’ll rarely see an American-style family kitchen with premium countertops, full-size appliances, and classic cupboards in one of these wooden homes. Instead, countertops are plain and compact, storage typically includes a couple of lower cabinets plus floating shelves, and small-to-medium appliances that are almost never seamlessly incorporated into the furniture.
These small kitchens are almost a perfect expression of the inherent bohemian spirit of French tiny homes – imperfect, but full of charm. In Tiny house Aigoual, placing the kitchen to one end of the layout could make it seem even smaller, cramped, and dark, but the builder has cleverly added one of the portholes here, for added luminosity, as well as choosing full glazing for the main entrance, to bring in even more light.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois The shape and design of the upper cupboards were also adapted to the limited space available, and an extra-small loft space above offers additional storage. Overall, this kitchen is so small that the bathroom fits right next to it, yet it’s fully equipped with all the essential appliances for permanent accommodation. The same applies to the bathroom, which has just enough floor space for a conventional toilet, an enclosed shower cabin, and a slim vanity with a tiny sink.
Tiny Aigoual’s lounge is intended for multi-functionality. Instead of a conventional sofa, it’s furnished with a custom-crafted bench, another bespoke feature that makes each of these wooden tiny homes unique. Apart from comfy seating, this bench can be turned into a two-person bed, and it also provides generous storage in the form of built-in drawers. With large windows on each side, as well as a beautiful porthole right above, this open lounge enjoys maximum light.
By avoiding bulky furniture and by placing windows in just the right areas, all around the house, this French builder has turned what could be considered a compact mobile home into a welcoming, peaceful oasis that looks much more spacious than its actual size. Natural light seems to embrace those inside wherever they are, including the loft bedroom.
This 6-square-meter (64.5 square feet) bedroom comes with the advantages that only bigger tiny house lofts typically offer. Most impressive: two large windows flanking the bed, plus a large round window on the wall behind the bed. Add to this ample walk-around space, and you get a loft that feels deliciously spacious, not to mention the quality and durability of its floor and walls, compared to cheaper versions.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois A mid-height safety wall adds just the right amount of privacy while keeping this bedroom as light-filled as the rest of the house, an oasis within an oasis. The sturdy staircase also contributes to the overall high comfort level, especially in the long run, compared to ladders or hybrid staircases. Plus, the staircase was crafted to hide ample storage space beneath a few doors, a more elegant solution than the standard open compartments.
From the delicate touch of the aluminum trims to the off-grid features and whimsical portholes, Aigoual stands out among French tiny homes – an excellent option that can house up to four people, providing comfortable and sustainable long-term accommodation.
